Findings.Comment: The function signature accepts a caller-provided `ctx`, and the doc comment explicitly states the caller's context bounds the whole operation. The diff replaces that context with `context.Background()` for both the HTTP request creation and body read. If a caller passes a context with a deadline or cancellation signal (e.g., from an HTTP handler with a timeout), the `FetchDiff` operation will ignore it, potentially blocking the caller indefinitely on a slow or hanging Bitbucket API response. This violates the documented contract and can cause goroutine leaks or timeouts at the caller level.
Findings.Headline: Caller context ignored — breaks documented contract
Findings.Suggestion: req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, u, nil)
Evidence: func (c *Client) FetchDiff(ctx context.Context, project, repo string, pr int) (string, error) {

Expected.why: ctx is a parameter but never used; context.Background() is passed to both NewRequestWithContext and getTextCapped, so the caller's timeout and cancellation cannot stop the request or the body read. Bitbucket has no Client.Timeout by design, which makes the caller's ctx the only bound on a 10 MiB diff.

Findings.Comment: The lock acquired at line 17 is not released when the team slug is not found. The error return at line 20 exits without unlocking, leaving the mutex locked. Any subsequent call to `Disable` (or other methods that acquire `r.mu`) will block forever, causing a deadlock.
Findings.Headline: Missing mutex unlock in error path of Disable method — deadlock

Expected.why: The Unlock now runs only on the success path, so returning the unknown-team error leaves r.mu locked and every subsequent caller blocks forever.

Findings.Comment: Removing the `return r.Body` from the nil-ticket branch causes execution to fall through to `r.Ticket.Key`, which dereferences the nil pointer and panics. On any call where `r` is non-nil but `r.Ticket` is nil, the program crashes with a nil pointer dereference. The comment claims a "shared renderer" handles the nil case, but no such code exists — the only code after the if-block is the direct dereference.
Findings.Headline: Nil-pointer dereference when Ticket is nil — crash on nil ticket
Evidence: // Ticket is optional; fall through to the shared renderer.

Expected.why: The nil branch no longer returns, so r.Ticket.Key panics whenever Ticket is nil. A reviewer may anchor on the dead check (19) or on the dereference (22).

Findings.Comment: The change from `last > len(lines)` to `last >= len(lines)` and setting `last = len(lines) + 1` creates an out-of-bounds slice condition. When `first + n` equals the length of `lines` (e.g., hunk ends at the file's last line and context request reaches exactly the end), the condition triggers, `last` becomes `len(lines) + 1`, and the subsequent slice `lines[first:last]` will panic at runtime because Go slice upper bounds are exclusive and cannot exceed the slice's length. For example, with a 5-line file where `first=0` and `n=5`, `last` becomes 6, causing a panic on the slice operation. This defeats the stated goal of stopping at the last line and introduces a runtime crash for edge-case inputs.
Findings.Headline: Off-by-one causes slice panic when context reaches EOF

Expected.why: The clamp sets last to len(lines)+1, so the final slice expression lines[first:last] runs one past the length. With no spare capacity that panics; with spare capacity it silently yields a phantom trailing line, which is the quieter half of the bug.
The response body is never closed on any path, so the underlying connection is leaked on every call, successful or not.

Finding.Comment: Removing `defer resp.Body.Close()` leaks the HTTP response body on every call. On early returns (non-2xx status or JSON decode failure) the body is never closed, and even on success the underlying TCP connection and file descriptor remain open. Under sustained load, this will exhaust file descriptors and break the client.
Finding.Headline: Resource leak: removed defer resp.Body.Close()

Findings.Comment: Removing the lock around `q.depth = len(q.pending)` creates a data race. The worker runs in its own goroutine while `Submit` and `Depth` also access `q.pending` and `q.depth` under the mutex. When the worker reads `q.pending` without holding the lock, it can race with `Submit` appending a new job, leading to a torn read of the slice's length header or seeing a stale internal pointer. This can cause `Depth()` to return an incorrect value and, in a worst case, corrupt the slice memory. The lock must be held for the duration of the `len(q.pending)` read and the subsequent `q.depth` assignment.
Findings.Headline: Data race on q.pending in worker goroutine — fix before merge

Expected.why: The worker goroutine writes q.depth and reads q.pending without holding q.mu, while Submit writes and Depth reads the same fields under the mutex; that is a data race.

Findings.Comment: The `tx.Commit(ctx)` return value is discarded. If the commit fails (e.g., due to a transient network error, serialization failure, or constraint violation discovered at commit time), `AddClaim` returns `nil`, leading the caller to believe the claim was persisted. This can cause silent data loss: the transaction is rolled back by the deferred `tx.Rollback`, but the caller proceeds as if the insert succeeded.
Findings.Headline: Commit error silently ignored — silent data loss

Expected.why: tx.Commit's error is discarded, so a failed commit is reported to the caller as success and the claim silently does not exist.

Findings.Comment: When `errNoRows` is detected (project has no owner), the code wraps and returns the raw `err` instead of `ErrNoClaim`. Callers matching on `ErrNoClaim` via `errors.Is` will never detect the "no claim" case, breaking the documented contract. Conversely, any non-no-rows database error now returns `ErrNoClaim`, masking real faults and violating the function's purpose of distinguishing "nobody owns it" from database errors.
Findings.Headline: Swapped error returns break ErrNoClaim contract for no-owner case — blocking

Expected.why: The branches wrap each other's error: errors.Is(err, ErrNoClaim) is now false when the project is genuinely unclaimed and true when the query failed, so a database fault is treated as an unowned project.
